topic: Strange places on the US-Canada border, led by the Haskell Free Library
hook: Your library card can work in two countries, and a black line on the floor marks the border.
title: Why the US-Canada Border Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
A library with a black line on the reading-room floor, a fort built in the wrong country, and a town you can only reach through Canada. These seven places on the US-Canada border look fake on a map, but every one of them is real. Watch to the end for the library where people sit in two countries at once.

#geography #borders #facts
comment_prompt: Which of these seven places would you visit first?

chapters.title: The fort built in the wrong country
The street split by the border

scenes.narration: Your library card can work in two countries, and a black line on the floor marks the border.
scenes.headline: A Library In Two Countries

scenes.narration: People sit on both sides of that line, reading quietly, and nobody checks a passport at the table.
scenes.headline: Sitting On The Border

scenes.narration: The US-Canada border is the longest between two countries, and it hides places that make no sense on a map.
scenes.headline: The Longest Border

scenes.narration: Today you will see a fort built in the wrong country, and a town you can only reach by driving through Canada.
scenes.headline: Wrong Country Fort

scenes.narration: You will see a patch of America sitting above Canada, and an island that both countries say is theirs.
scenes.headline: An Island Both Claim

scenes.narration: Seven places, each one stranger than the last, and every single one of them is real.
scenes.headline: Seven Real Places

scenes.narration: By the end, you will step inside that library and see the black line on the floor yourself.
scenes.headline: The Black Line

scenes.narration: Number one: a fort that America built in Canada by mistake, and then had to give up.
scenes.headline: Fort Blunder

scenes.narration: In the early 1800s, the United States started building a big fort at Rouses Point, in New York state.
scenes.headline: A Fort Begins

scenes.narration: The border there follows a line of latitude, the forty-fifth parallel, and the plan was to build just south of it.
scenes.headline: The 45th Parallel

scenes.narration: But the first survey was wrong. When it was checked again, the half-built fort stood on British land.
scenes.headline: The Survey Was Wrong

scenes.narration: Work stopped at once. A fort meant to guard America was sitting on the wrong side of the line.
scenes.headline: Work Stops

scenes.narration: People started calling it Fort Blunder, and the name stuck for good.
scenes.headline: Fort Blunder

scenes.narration: The problem was fixed in 1842, when a treaty gave that small piece of land to the United States.
scenes.headline: Fixed In 1842

scenes.narration: A new fort, Fort Montgomery, was later built on that spot, right beside Lake Champlain.
scenes.headline: Fort Montgomery

scenes.narration: This was long before GPS, so surveyors measured the land with chains and instruments, and small errors could be huge.
scenes.headline: Before GPS

scenes.narration: So the first surprise is that this border was once drawn by careful guesses, and guesses can be wrong.
scenes.headline: Careful Guesses

scenes.narration: But it gets stranger. Next is a piece of America that you cannot drive to without crossing Canada.
scenes.headline: Stranger Ahead

scenes.narration: Number two: a town where even a trip home by road means crossing an international border.
scenes.headline: Point Roberts

scenes.narration: Point Roberts is a small piece of Washington state, hanging off the end of a Canadian peninsula.
scenes.headline: A Piece Of Washington

scenes.narration: The border was drawn along the forty-ninth parallel, and that straight line cut right through the land.
scenes.headline: A Line Cuts Through

scenes.narration: That straight line, the forty-ninth parallel, runs across much of the western border between the two countries.
scenes.headline: A Very Straight Line

scenes.narration: So the southern tip ended up American, while everything joined to it by land is Canadian.
scenes.headline: American Tip

scenes.narration: To drive from Point Roberts to the rest of America, you must go through Canada and show your documents.
scenes.headline: Cross Canada To Go Home

scenes.narration: Imagine going to the next city in your own state, but you have to cross a border first.
scenes.headline: Imagine That

scenes.narration: It is a piece of one country that you can only reach by land through another.
scenes.headline: Land Through Another

scenes.narration: The same kind of line also made an even stranger oddity, far to the east, in Minnesota.
scenes.headline: Even Stranger

scenes.narration: Number three: a piece of Minnesota that sits north of the border line, all on its own.
scenes.headline: Northwest Angle

scenes.narration: It is called the Northwest Angle, and it is the northernmost point of the lower forty-eight US states.
scenes.headline: Northernmost Point

scenes.narration: Its odd shape comes from a mapping mistake. The treaty of 1783 relied on a map that got the geography wrong.
scenes.headline: A Map Mistake

scenes.narration: Negotiators believed the Mississippi began further north than it really does, so the line they described did not fit the land.
scenes.headline: Wrong River Source

scenes.narration: Later talks fixed the problem by following the water, and that left this odd corner of land attached to Minnesota.
scenes.headline: A Leftover Corner

scenes.narration: By land, the only road to it runs through Manitoba, in Canada. Many visitors cross the lake by boat instead.
scenes.headline: Road Through Canada

scenes.narration: It is a part of America with Canada on its land side and a huge lake on the other.
scenes.headline: Lake On One Side

scenes.narration: So far, these are borders that were drawn wrong. The next place is a town where the border barely matters.
scenes.headline: Almost No Border

scenes.narration: If you like strange places like these, subscribe, because tomorrow's video is just as odd.
scenes.headline: More Strange Places

scenes.narration: Number four: an Alaskan town where the only road out leads straight into Canada.
scenes.headline: Hyder, Alaska

scenes.narration: Hyder, Alaska, sits at the end of a road in the far southeast of the state.
scenes.headline: End Of The Road

scenes.narration: That road does not connect to any other Alaskan town. It runs to Stewart, a Canadian town in British Columbia.
scenes.headline: The Road To Stewart

scenes.narration: When you drive from Canada into Hyder, there is no US customs booth waiting for you.
scenes.headline: No Booth Entering

scenes.narration: Heading back the other way, Canadian officers check you at the border crossing.
scenes.headline: Checked Going Back

scenes.narration: Hyder depends on Stewart for many everyday things, and the two towns feel almost like one place.
scenes.headline: Two Towns, One Life

scenes.narration: Hyder even keeps the same clock as Stewart, Pacific time, while the rest of Alaska runs an hour behind.
scenes.headline: Same Clock As Canada

scenes.narration: Two towns, two countries, one shared clock, and only one road in or out.
scenes.headline: One Road In

scenes.narration: Now picture something even smaller: a rocky island in the sea that both countries say is theirs.
scenes.headline: A Rock Both Want

scenes.narration: Number five: a puffin island that the United States and Canada both claim.
scenes.headline: Machias Seal Island

scenes.narration: Machias Seal Island sits in the Gulf of Maine, between the coast of Maine and New Brunswick.
scenes.headline: Gulf Of Maine

scenes.narration: Nobody has settled who owns it, so the waters around it are called the Grey Zone.
scenes.headline: The Grey Zone

scenes.narration: Canada keeps a lighthouse on the island with keepers, while the United States still says the island is American.
scenes.headline: Canada's Lighthouse

scenes.narration: The island is famous for its Atlantic puffins, small birds with bright orange beaks that nest there each summer.
scenes.headline: Puffins Nest Here

scenes.narration: The puffins, of course, have no idea which country they belong to.
scenes.headline: Puffins Don't Care

scenes.narration: Tour boats carry visitors to see the birds, and everyone lives with the dispute year after year.
scenes.headline: Boats Of Visitors

scenes.narration: Lobster fishing in the waters around it is the real prize, and fishermen on both sides keep a close watch.
scenes.headline: The Lobster Prize

scenes.narration: Yet there is no gunfire. The two countries have not fought a war against each other since 1812.
scenes.headline: A Polite Dispute

scenes.narration: Next, the place where that peace is easiest to see, because the border runs down the middle of a street.
scenes.headline: A Street Border

scenes.narration: Number six: a street where one side of the road is America and the other side is Canada.
scenes.headline: Canusa Street

scenes.narration: In Derby Line, Vermont, and Stanstead, Quebec, two towns have grown together into one community.
scenes.headline: Derby Line & Stanstead

scenes.narration: Canusa Street is named for Canada and USA, and the border runs along it.
scenes.headline: CAN + USA

scenes.narration: Houses on one side of the street are in the United States, and the houses opposite are in Canada.
scenes.headline: Houses In Two Countries
scenes.visual_query: houses on both sides of street

scenes.narration: Neighbours can wave across the road, but crossing it without going through border control is not allowed.
scenes.headline: Wave, Don't Cross

scenes.narration: Before the world changed after 2001, people in these towns crossed far more freely to visit friends and shops.
scenes.headline: Before 2001

scenes.narration: Today there are rules and officers, but the two towns still feel like one community.
scenes.headline: One Community

scenes.narration: And right in the middle of that community stands a building that sits on both sides of the line.
scenes.headline: A Building On The Line

scenes.narration: Number seven, the strangest of all: a library where you can sit in two countries at once.
scenes.headline: The Haskell Library

scenes.narration: The Haskell Free Library and Opera House opened in 1904, right on the border between Derby Line and Stanstead.
scenes.headline: Opened In 1904

scenes.narration: The front door is in Canada, but a lot of the books are on the American side.
scenes.headline: Door In Canada

scenes.narration: Inside the reading room, a black line runs across the floor. That line is the border.
scenes.headline: The Black Line

scenes.narration: Imagine reading a book in a quiet room, then glancing down to see a country border between your feet.
scenes.headline: A Border Underfoot

scenes.narration: A reader can sit at a table on one side of the line while a friend sits on the other.
scenes.headline: Friends In Two Countries

scenes.narration: Upstairs is an opera house too. The stage is in the United States, while most of the seats are in Canada.
scenes.headline: Stage In The USA

scenes.narration: So the audience watches a show in one country while the actors perform in another.
scenes.headline: Audience In Canada

scenes.narration: The building was meant to be shared by both towns, and it has stayed open to both communities.
scenes.headline: Built To Share

scenes.narration: Visitors from Canada walk in through the front door, and they are expected to leave the same way.
scenes.headline: Leave The Way You Came

scenes.narration: There is no passport counter at the door, yet the rules about where you may walk are real.
scenes.headline: Rules Still Apply

scenes.narration: That is the real surprise on this border: a line the size of a strip of tape that both countries respect.
scenes.headline: A Line Like Tape

scenes.narration: So here is the loop. Your library card can work in two countries, and a black line on the floor marks the border.
scenes.headline: Two Countries, One Room

scenes.narration: Fort Blunder, Point Roberts, the Northwest Angle, Hyder, the Grey Zone, Canusa Street and the Haskell Library, all on one border.
scenes.headline: Seven Strange Places

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: another place that looks fake on the map but is completely real.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow: Another One
